Augusto Pinochet. The Chilean military officer who orchestrated a coup against Salvador Allende in 1973 and ruled Chile as dictator for seventeen years. His regime was marked by severe human-rights abuses, disappearances, torture, and economic neoliberal reforms that reshaped the nation.

Pinochet led the military coup on September 11, 1973, that overthrew Allende's democratically elected socialist government. He established the Junta, a military ruling council, and served as its leader. In 1974, he declared himself president and ruled until 1990. To consolidate power, Pinochet relied on the secret police, DINA, which carried out widespread torture, extrajudicial killings, and forced disappearances of political opponents. Economically, he implemented neoliberal policies, privatizing state industries and replacing Allende's socialism with a free-market model. In 1990, Pinochet stepped down after losing a plebiscite, but remained Commander-in-Chief of the army until 1998. After leaving office, he was indicted for human-rights crimes in Spain and Chile. He died in 2006 before facing full prosecution.
